remaining_concerns: Most direct evidence is legal and status-based rather than operational, so it supports non-nuclear posture more strongly than any exercised command capacity.
Several records are derivative, retrospective, or adjacent-topic corroboration, so the UN and IAEA records carry the most weight.
Several peace-process and official items show stated intent or institutional action, not proof of battlefield outcomes.
Humanitarian records document severe civilian harm and displacement, but usually do not assign direct presidential responsibility.
Attribution of external support and proxy dynamics remains contested in some reports, so those claims should stay cautious.
Eastern DRC violence is still heavily driven by armed groups, so attribution to Tshisekedi is mostly indirect and framed through protection failures rather than direct orders.
Several retained sources are retrospective country reports or humanitarian syntheses, so the record is stronger on pattern than on precise command responsibility for each incident.
The packet is heavy on repression and institutional-weakness evidence, with limited favorable or balancing material.
Several items are broad system-level summaries rather than direct acts by Tshisekedi, so attribution remains partly indirect.
Only one clear incident cluster is strongly represented (Kabund and media pressure); other mechanisms are under-sampled.
Direct performance evidence is strongest on macro management, fiscal governance, transparency, corruption, and rights conditions; welfare and delivery outcomes remain partly indirect or contextual.
Several official budget items are useful as declared intent, but they do not establish implementation quality on their own.
The corruption and rights record is supported by strong external reporting, but some incidents are single-case illustrations rather than full-sector coverage.
Evidence remains heavily humanitarian and donor/IGO sourced, so direct ruler attribution is often moderate rather than strong.
Education and health are well covered, but social protection and governance evidence is still mostly baseline or programmatic rather than outcome-heavy.
Several strong claims are retrospective or project-level, so the chapter still depends on contextual inference rather than many directly ruler-attributable outcomes.
Repression and accountability failures remain documented despite limited reform signals.
Corruption evidence is strongest in associate/network and institutional records, not in direct proof of Tshisekedi personal enrichment.
Several positive institutional steps are promises or commissions rather than demonstrated implementation.
Several positive records are official self-reporting and still need independent outcome corroboration.
The peace-process cluster shows repeated diplomacy and ceasefire announcements, but not durable compliance or battlefield results.
The corruption cluster is strong on allegations and audits, but some items remain investigative or administrative rather than adjudicated findings.
Budget and program documents show intent and allocation, but implementation quality and distributional effects are only partly evidenced here.
